title: Anthropic Extends Invisible Text Watermarks to Older Claude Models Starting November 3
summary: Anthropic extends invisible text watermarks to older Claude models starting November 3
detailed: Anthropic is extending its invisible text watermarking to legacy Claude models—including Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6—starting November 3.
The machine-readable statistical signature is embedded via word choice patterns to survive ordinary document handling and support compliance with regulations like the EU AI Act.
The watermark indicates the model touched the content rather than authored it, and detection tool access remains limited to vetted regulators, researchers, and enterprises.
sentences: Anthropic has begun notifying customers that its invisible text watermarking will reach its legacy Claude models on November 3, widening a provenance system the company first announced in August 2026.
The change means output from several older versions of the chatbot will carry a machine-readable statistical signature even though the text itself looks unchanged.
The affected models, according to the customer notice, are Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6.

When Anthropic introduced the watermarking policy earlier this year, only models released from August onward, including Claude Opus 5.5, received the treatment; the company said at the time that earlier versions would be brought into line on a rolling basis.
The watermark is designed to leave meaning, quality and readability untouched.

It travels with text when it is copied and pasted elsewhere, and it can persist through a degree of editing, which is the practical point: the mark is meant to survive the ordinary handling of a document rather than only the moment of generation.
Anthropic has framed the rollout as a global measure, applying in the United States and Japan as well as the European Union, where the labeling requirement stems from the EU AI Act.
Note: Model list and effective date are drawn from Anthropic's customer notification as reported by AI strategist Pete Sena.
Detection is not a public utility.

The checking tool sits in a private preview aimed at regulators, news organizations, fact-checkers, researchers, educational institutions and companies with compliance obligations, and access is limited to parties that have been vetted.
That asymmetry has drawn scrutiny: the people whose documents carry the mark generally cannot verify it themselves.
That gap is sharpest in cases where Claude is used for light editing rather than authoring.
A user who runs a translation, a proofread or a rewrite through the model can end up with a watermarked document even though the substance was written by a person.
Anthropic's help materials acknowledge the distinction, noting that a watermark indicates the model touched the content, not that it composed it.
In practice the two outcomes may be hard to separate for anyone reading a detection result.
Technical observers have raised a further point about durability.
Because the signal is embedded in patterns of word choice rather than in visible characters, processing a text through a different model instructed to paraphrase everything can strip it out.
That creates a split between users who know how to remove the mark and those who do not, including students, job applicants and people writing in a second language.
The watermarking expansion lands alongside other recent changes to Anthropic's guardrails.

The company has tightened Claude Code, its programming tool, to stop users from rebuilding specific existing video games, even when a project is renamed or presented as original; original games, genre games and projects built on a user's own designs and assets remain permitted.

Anthropic staff said the aim is to steer the model away from reproducing someone else's title because using Claude to infringe intellectual property violates its usage policy, and that the company will keep iterating on the balance.

The restriction follows a wave of AI-assisted decompilations of major titles that have circulated as browser-playable fan projects, and it comes after Anthropic agreed last year to a $1.5 billion class-action settlement with authors who accused it of training on copyrighted material.

Separately, the company added language to its usage policy in early October barring users from sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward its models, a rule that in extreme cases could lead to a permanent ban.

A spokesperson said the main enforcement mechanism remains Claude ending a conversation, and that the prohibition does not target people expressing frustration, giving blunt feedback, or conducting testing and research.

Critics mocked the provision as treating software as a sentient being, while supporters argued that hostile inputs can degrade model behavior and that permitting cruelty toward interactive systems carries broader social costs.
The immediate market effect of broader watermarking is likely to be felt in verification workflows rather than in model pricing.

Enterprises with EU exposure now have a clearer compliance story for content produced on older Claude versions, which matters for firms that standardized on those models before August and have been unable to certify provenance.
For media and publishing customers, the private detection preview offers a way to screen submissions, though its restricted access limits independent auditing.

For Anthropic, which is expected to go public this month, the rollout is also a positioning move: it lets the company present itself as the vendor with the most developed provenance infrastructure at a moment when regulators in Brussels and elsewhere are pressing for machine-readable labeling.

The risk is that a mark most users cannot see or check invites suspicion rather than trust, particularly if third-party AI detectors begin claiming to read signals the company says only vetted reviewers can access.
Whether the older-model watermark holds up under real-world editing is the question that will determine its usefulness.

Anthropic has said the mark can survive some modification but has not published durability benchmarks, and the detection tool's closed status means outside researchers cannot test those claims independently.
Until that changes, the policy's reach will be easier to measure than its reliability.
